items.title: Lesson 3 "Identify" (Figure 15, plasma sphere): A fluorescent tube glows when it is plugged in. Identify the cause of the electric field inside the tube.

answer.html: The field is caused by the charges on the two electrodes at the ends of the tube, which are connected to the power supply and held at different potentials (one end is positive while the other is negative, alternating with the AC supply). That field accelerates the free electrons and ions in the gas, and their collisions make the tube glow.

items.title: Lesson 3 "Get It?" (strength of a field): Explain how you would determine both the strength and the direction of the electric field at a point near a charged doorknob.

body.html: Place a small positive test charge 𝑞′ at the point and measure the force 𝐹 on it. The strength is 𝐸= 𝐹/ 𝑞′. The direction of the field is the direction of the force on the positive test charge.

answer.html: Measure the force on a small positive test charge and divide by its charge, 𝐸= 𝐹/ 𝑞′ (in N/C); the field points the way the force on the positive test charge points.

items.title: 24 (Example Problem 2 Practice 1): A positive test charge of 3.2 × 10−6 C feels a force of 7.4 × 10−4 N. What is the magnitude of the electric field at that point?

body.html: 𝑞′ = 3.2 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> C, 𝐹= 7.4 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>4</sup> N. Unknown: 𝐸.
The field is the force per unit test charge.

items.title: 25 (Example Problem 2 Practice 2): A charge of −4.5 × 10−8 C feels a 0.036 N force directed upward. Find the field's magnitude and direction.

body.html: 𝑞= −4.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>8</sup> C, 𝐹= 0.036 N upward.
The field points in the direction of the force on a positive charge. The force on a negative charge points opposite the field.
The force is upward on a negative charge, so the field is downward.

answer.html: 8.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> N/C, directed downward.

check.html: This is below the field that makes a spark in air (3 × 10<sup>6</sup> N/C), so it is strong but plausible.

items.title: 26 (Example Problem 2 Practice 3): A 6.5 × 10−7 C positive charge sits in a 42 N/C field directed west. Find the force on it.

body.html: 𝐹= 𝑞𝐸= (6.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>7</sup> C)(42 N/C) = 2.7 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> N. For a positive charge the force is in the field direction.

answer.html: 2.7 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> N toward the west.

items.title: 27 (Example Problem 2 Practice 4, Table 2): Complete the table, where each row is a test charge in an electric field.

body.html: 𝐸= 𝐹/ 𝑞′ in each row; solve for whichever quantity is missing.

answer.html: Row 1: 2.5 × 10<sup>5</sup> N/C; Row 2: 0.48 N; Row 3: 3.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> C.

check.html: All three test charges are a few microcoulombs and all fields are of order 10<sup>5</sup> N/C, so the numbers are consistent.

items.title: 28 (Example Problem 2 Practice 5, Figure 17): A negative test charge 𝑞′ = −5.0 × 10−6 C feels a force of 0.13 N directed toward a positive source charge 𝑞. Find the field magnitude and its direction at the test charge.

body.html: |𝑞′ | = 5.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> C, 𝐹= 0.13 N toward 𝑞.
𝐸= 𝐹/ | 𝑞′|. The force on a negative charge is opposite the field.

answer.html: 2.6 × 10<sup>4</sup> N/C. The field points away from the positive charge 𝑞 (opposite to the force on the negative test charge).

items.title: 29 (Example Problem 2 Practice 6, Challenge): You map the field of an unknown charge with a 4.0 × 10−7 C test charge, and then with a 1.2 × 10−6 C test charge. (a) Are the forces the same? (b) Are the field strengths the same?

body.html: 𝐹= 𝑞′𝐸, and 𝐸= 𝐾𝑞/ 𝑟<sup>2</sup> depends only on the source charge and location. Work (a): At the same place the field is the same, so 𝐹= 𝑞′𝐸 is proportional to the test charge. The ratio of the charges is (1.2 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup>) / (4.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>7</sup>) = 3.0, so the larger test charge feels three times the force. Work (b): 𝐸= 𝐹/ 𝑞′: when 𝑞′ triples, 𝐹 triples, so the ratio is unchanged.

answer.html: No. The force is proportional to the test charge, so the larger test charge feels three times the force. Answer (b): Yes. The field strength is 𝐹/ 𝑞′, which does not depend on the test charge; both maps give the same field.

items.title: 30 (Example Problem 3 Practice 1): Find the electric field magnitude 0.85 m from a 6.4 × 10−6 C point charge.

body.html: 𝐸∝1 / 𝑟<sup>2</sup>, so tripling 𝑟 gives 𝐸/ 9: (7.97 × 10<sup>4</sup>) / 9 = 8.9 × 10<sup>3</sup> N/C (direct check: 𝐾𝑞/ (2.55 m)<sup>2</sup> = 8.86 × 10<sup>3</sup>).

items.title: 32 (Example Problem 3 Practice 3): Find the electric field 2.4 m west of a −5.5 × 10−6 C point charge.

body.html: 𝐸= (9.0 × 10<sup>9</sup>)(5.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup>) / (2.4)<sup>2</sup> = 8.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> N/C. The charge is negative, so the field points toward it; the point is west of the charge, so toward the charge is east.

answer.html: 8.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> N/C toward the east (toward the charge).

answer.html: 𝑞= + 1.1 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>8</sup> C (positive)

body.html: Coulomb's law gives the force on the test charge: 𝐹= 𝐾𝑄𝑞′ / 𝑟<sup>2</sup>. The field is the force per unit test charge:
The factor 𝑞′ cancels, leaving only 𝑄 and 𝑟. Numerically: 𝐹<sub>1</sub> = (9.0 × 10<sup>9</sup>)(2.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup>)(1.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>9</sup>)

items.title: 36 (Example Problem 3 Practice 7, Figure 18): A test charge sits 3.5 m from a point charge 𝑞= + 2.4 × 10−6 C. Find the field magnitude and direction at the test charge.

answer.html: 1.8 × 10<sup>3</sup> N/C, directed away from the positive charge 𝑞 (the direction of the force on a positive test charge).

items.title: 37 (Example Problem 3 Practice 8, Challenge): A −3.5 × 10−6 C sphere sits at one corner of a square that is 2.5 m on each side. Find the field at the opposite corner.

body.html: The distance is the square's diagonal: 𝑟= √2 (2.5 m), so 𝑟<sup>2</sup> = 2(2.5)<sup>2</sup> = 12.5 m<sup>2</sup> .

answer.html: 2.5 × 10<sup>3</sup> N/C (pointing directly toward the sphere, since it is negative).

items.title: Lesson 3 "CCC: Cause and Effect" (Figures 19 and 20): Two equal negative point charges sit side by side. How does knowing the field of a single negative charge help you predict the field pattern of the pair, including any place where the field is zero?

answer.html: A single negative charge produces radial field lines pointing inward. The field of the pair is the vector sum of the two single-charge fields, so far away it looks like one negative charge, with lines bending away from the gap between the charges. At the midpoint the two inward fields are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so they cancel and the net field there is zero.

items.title: Lesson 3 "CCC: Patterns" (Figures 19 and 20): How can the field pattern of two oppositely charged parallel plates help explain a thundercloud above flat ground and the membrane of a nerve cell?

answer.html: In each case two oppositely charged surfaces, a cloud base and the ground, or the inside and outside of a membrane, are close together compared with their size. Between them the field lines are straight, parallel, and evenly spaced, which means the field is uniform and has the same strength everywhere in the gap. Recognizing the pattern tells you the field is 𝐸= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑑 and that a charge between the surfaces feels the same force anywhere, at a scale of kilometers or of nanometers.

items.title: Lesson 3 "Describe" (Figure 20): A +𝑄 charge and a −𝑄 charge are held 10 cm apart. Describe where a small charge would feel the largest and the smallest force: at the midpoint, 2 cm from +𝑄 on the line between them, or 50 cm away from both.

answer.html: The force is greatest where field lines are closest together: very near either charge, so the point 2 cm from +𝑄 has the largest force. At the midpoint the lines are less dense, but the two fields add (both point from +𝑄 toward −𝑄), so the force there is moderate. At 50 cm the lines are far apart and the two fields largely cancel, so the force is smallest.

items.title: 38 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 3): Describe how to map the electric field around a charged sphere. Say how you find the magnitude at each point, and what happens if the test charge you use is much larger than the sphere's charge.

answer.html: Detect: move a small test charge to each point; where it feels a force, there is a field, and the field points the way the force on a positive test charge points. Magnitude: 𝐸= 𝐹/ 𝑞′. If the test charge is large, its own field pushes the charges on the sphere around, which changes the field you are trying to measure; so the test charge must be small, but large enough to give a measurable force.

items.title: 39 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 3): A negative test charge of −1.80 × 10−8 C feels a force of 4.50 × 10−3 N toward the south. Find the field.

body.html: 𝐸= 𝐹/ | 𝑞′ | = (4.50 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> N) / (1.80 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>8</sup> C) = 2.50 × 10<sup>5</sup> N/C. The test charge is negative, so the field points opposite the force: toward the north.

answer.html: 2.50 × 10<sup>5</sup> N/C toward the north.

items.title: 40 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 3): In a field-line diagram, 16 lines leave charge X and 8 lines end on charge Y. What are the signs of X and Y, and how do their charge magnitudes compare?

answer.html: Field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative charges, so X is positive and Y is negative. The number of lines is proportional to the size of the charge, so |𝑞<sub>𝑋</sub>| is twice |𝑞<sub>𝑌</sub>| (the other 8 lines from X go off to other charges or far away).

items.title: 41 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 3): Two unlike charges are pulled farther apart. What happens to the energy stored in the field, and where does that energy come from?

answer.html: The energy in the field increases. The charges attract, so you must do work to pull them apart; that work is stored as energy in the field. (If they were released, the field would do work and the stored energy would decrease as they moved together.)

items.title: 42 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 3, Critical Thinking): A student wants to measure the field near a sphere carrying +2.0 × 10−9 C by using a test charge of +8.0 × 10−6 C on a light ball. Is that test charge small enough?

body.html: The test charge is (8.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup>) / (2.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>9</sup>) = 4.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> times larger than the sphere's charge. A proper test charge should have a negligible effect on the charges that produce the field. A charge this large would repel the charges on the sphere (and any mobile charge in nearby objects) and move them, changing the field being measured.

answer.html: No. The test charge is thousands of times larger than the source charge, so its field would disturb the charges producing the field and the measurement would not be accurate.

items.title: Lesson 3 "Identify Crosscutting Concepts" and "Review the News" (activities): Start a crosscutting-concepts table using Lesson 2, and describe how you would review a news story about static electricity causing fires at grain elevators or fuel stations.

A good write-up names the source, states the main finding about charge buildup and discharge in one or two sentences, and evaluates the source (author, date, evidence, bias).

items.title: Lesson 3 "Identify" (Figure 15, plasma sphere) Question: Identify the cause of the electric field inside the plasma sphere.

answer.html: The field is caused by the charged central electrode, whose net charge alternates rapidly between positive and negative. That field accelerates the ions in the gas, making the glowing streams.

items.title: Lesson 3 "CCC: Cause and Effect" (Figures 19 and 20) Question: How does modeling simple fields from single point charges help predict fields from multiple

answer.html: A single positive or negative charge produces a simple radial pattern (Figure 19, left and middle). The field of several charges is the vector sum of the single-charge fields, so you can build the complex pattern from the simple ones: the mixed-charge pattern in Figure 19 looks like outward lines from the positive charge bending into the two negative charges, and the grass seeds in Figure 20 show lines running from one charge to its opposite for unlike charges, and bending away from each other, with a weak (zero) region between, for like charges.

items.title: Lesson 3 "CCC: Patterns" (Figures 19 and 20) Question: How can field-line patterns help explain phenomena at different scales?

answer.html: The same patterns appear at many scales: radial lines around a single charge (an ion, an electron near an atom, a charged sphere), dipole patterns between a positive and negative charge (a polar molecule, two charged plates), and strong, closely spaced lines at points (lightning rods, charged tips). Recognizing the pattern tells you where the force is strong, where it is weak, and which way charges move, for lightning, for a water molecule, or for a charged balloon.

items.title: Lesson 3 "Describe" (Figure 20) Question: How do the models show where charged particles would feel more or less force?

answer.html: Field lines (and grass seeds) are closer together where the field is stronger, so a charge feels more force there: near the charges, and along lines joining unlike charges. Where lines are far apart, or absent as at the center between two like charges, the force is weaker or zero.

items.title: 38 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 3) Question: How do you detect a field at a point, find its magnitude, and choose the test charge?

answer.html: Detect: place a small charge there; if it feels a force, a field exists. Magnitude: 𝐸= 𝐹/ 𝑞′ using the measured force and the test charge. Choice of test charge: make it small enough that its own field does not push the source charges around and distort the field you are measuring (but large enough to produce a measurable force).

items.title: 39 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 3) Question: A positive test charge of 2.40 × 10−8 C feels 1.50 × 10−3 N toward the east. Find the field.

body.html: 𝐸= 𝐹/ 𝑞′ = (1.50 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> N) / (2.40 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>8</sup> C) = 6.25 × 10<sup>4</sup> N/C. The test charge is positive, so the field is in the same direction as the force.

answer.html: 6.25 × 10<sup>4</sup> N/C toward the east.

items.title: 40 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 3) Question: How can you tell which charges are positive and which negative from field lines?

answer.html: Field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative charges, so lines leaving a charge mark it as positive; lines ending on it mark it as negative.

items.title: 41 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 3) Question: When two charges interacting through a field change relative position, what happens to the

answer.html: The energy stored in the field changes. It increases when work is done to move the charges apart against attraction (or together against repulsion), and it decreases when the field does the work (the charges move as the force pushes them).

items.title: 42 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 3, Critical Thinking) Question: In Figure 19 (far right: a positive charge above two negative charges), is the top charge small

question.html: enough to be a test charge for the field of the two negative charges?

body.html: In the figure the top charge has many field lines of its own, and the lines from it bend strongly toward the negatives, so its field is comparable to those of the negative charges. A proper test charge should have a negligible effect on the charges producing the field; a charge this large would attract the two negative charges and move them, changing the field being measured.

answer.html: No. The top charge is too large; its own field is comparable to those of the others and would disturb the charges producing the field, so it would not give an accurate measurement.
